epa-608-readiness-check-type-1-016.explanation: A 7-ounce factory-sealed dehumidifier is a small appliance (5 pounds or less). With recovery equipment made after November 15, 1993, it must give up 80% of its charge when the compressor does not run (90% when it runs) or be pulled to 4 inches of Hg vacuum; with a dead compressor, self-contained (active) equipment is the practical way to get there.

distractorExplanations.b: 10 inches Hg vacuum comes from the high-pressure appliance table; the small-appliance vacuum option is 4 inches.
distractorExplanations.c: 7 ounces is far under the 5-pound limit, so the factory-sealed unit stays a small appliance under Type I, not Type II.
distractorExplanations.d: Passive recovery is allowed on small appliances, but it must still reach 80% recovered or 4 inches Hg vacuum, not any achievable level.

epa-608-readiness-check-type-1-018.prompt: A technician is servicing a small appliance that contains R-12 refrigerant. The recovery equipment has pulled the appliance down to 25 inches of mercury vacuum. What, if anything, must the technician still do to meet the EPA recovery requirement?
epa-608-readiness-check-type-1-018.explanation: For small appliances the vacuum option is 4 inches of mercury vacuum (the alternative is 80% or 90% of the charge recovered). A reading of 25 inches Hg vacuum is far deeper than 4 inches, so the requirement is already met and no further recovery step is needed.

distractorExplanations.a: The small-appliance level is 4 inches Hg vacuum, not 4 inches absolute; 25 inches of vacuum is already deeper, so no conversion check is needed.
distractorExplanations.b: 29.9 inches Hg vacuum is near a perfect vacuum and is not the small-appliance recovery level for any refrigerant.
distractorExplanations.d: Small-appliance percentage options are 90% (compressor running) or 80% (not running), not 95%, and the 25-inch vacuum already meets the rule.

options.a: No recovery required since the repair can be completed in under 30 minutes
options.b: Recover refrigerant to 0 psig before opening the system
options.c: Recover refrigerant to 10 inches of mercury vacuum before opening the system
options.d: Only recover refrigerant from the condenser section being replaced

epa-608-readiness-check-type-2-024.explanation: An R-22 appliance holding less than 200 pounds must be evacuated to 0 psig before it is opened, whether the recovery machine was built before or after November 15, 1993. Replacing the condenser coil is a major repair, but 0 psig still applies; 10 inches is the level for R-22 units of 200 pounds or more.

distractorExplanations.a: Recovery before opening the circuit is required for any repair length; a 30-minute job gets no exemption under the Section 608 evacuation rules.
distractorExplanations.c: 10 inches Hg vacuum is the level for R-22 appliances of 200 pounds or more (or other high-pressure units under 200 lb), not an 8-pound R-22 split system.
distractorExplanations.d: A split system's condenser coil cannot be valved off from the rest of the charge, so the circuit being opened must be recovered to 0 psig.

epa-608-readiness-check-core-032.prompt: A technician is preparing to recover refrigerant from an industrial chiller and finds that the borrowed recovery machine, built in 2015, has no label showing certification by an EPA-approved equipment testing organization. What must the technician do before proceeding?

options.a: Use the machine anyway, since the technician's own certification covers any equipment used
options.b: Use the equipment only if it passes a visual inspection for obvious defects
options.c: Obtain properly certified recovery equipment before beginning any recovery operations
options.d: Proceed if the system holds under 15 pounds, then have the machine tested afterward

epa-608-readiness-check-core-032.explanation: Recovery and recycling equipment made after November 15, 1993 must be certified by an EPA-approved testing organization (such as AHRI or UL) and labeled. That certification belongs to the equipment model and does not expire, but an unlabeled machine cannot be used, so certified equipment must be obtained first.

distractorExplanations.a: Technician certification and equipment certification are separate requirements; a certified technician still needs certified recovery equipment.
distractorExplanations.b: Visual inspection cannot substitute for proper certification; EPA requires formal certification that includes performance testing and verification.
distractorExplanations.d: There is no small-charge exemption to the certified-equipment rule, and testing the machine after the job does not make using it legal.

epa-608-readiness-check-type-1-012.prompt: A technician is using passive recovery methods on a small appliance refrigerator with a burned-out compressor. After 30 minutes, the system pressure has stabilized at 2 inches of mercury vacuum. What should the technician do next?

options.a: Continue passive recovery for another 30 minutes to reach the required vacuum level
options.b: Switch to active recovery to reach the required 4 inches of mercury vacuum
options.c: Document that recovery is complete since passive methods have achieved maximum extraction
options.d: Add nitrogen to pressurize the system and restart the passive recovery process

epa-608-readiness-check-type-1-012.explanation: With the compressor not running, a small appliance must have 80% of its charge recovered or be pulled to 4 inches of Hg vacuum. A stable 2-inch reading means passive recovery has stalled short of that level, so the technician switches to self-contained (active) equipment to finish.

distractorExplanations.a: Continuing passive recovery will not achieve a deeper vacuum since the system has already stabilized at 2 inches, which is insufficient for non-functioning compressor requirements.
distractorExplanations.c: A passive method reaching its limit does not end the duty; recovery must still reach 80% or 4 inches Hg vacuum for a non-running compressor.
distractorExplanations.d: Adding nitrogen would contaminate the refrigerant and is not an approved method for improving recovery efficiency in small appliances.

epa-608-readiness-check-type-1-033.prompt: A technician has completed refrigerant recovery from a small appliance window air conditioner containing 3 ounces of R-22. Using self-contained recovery equipment, the final system pressure reads 2 inches of mercury vacuum. The customer wants to dispose of the unit immediately. What must the technician do?

options.a: Continue recovery until reaching 4 inches of mercury vacuum
options.b: Release the unit for disposal, since 2 inches meets the small-appliance level
options.c: Wait 5 minutes, and if the reading holds, release the unit for disposal
options.d: Switch to system-dependent recovery and pull to 10 inches of mercury

epa-608-readiness-check-type-1-033.explanation: Small appliances must have 80% or 90% of the charge recovered (compressor off or on) or be pulled to 4 inches of Hg vacuum. A 2-inch vacuum reading is shallower than 4 inches, so recovery must continue before the unit goes for disposal.

distractorExplanations.b: 2 inches of vacuum is shallower than the 4-inch small-appliance level, so the unit is not ready for disposal yet.
distractorExplanations.c: A stable reading does not matter if the required level has not been reached; recovery must continue first.
distractorExplanations.d: 10 inches Hg vacuum is a high-pressure appliance level, and switching methods does not change the small-appliance target.

epa-608-readiness-check-type-1-050.prompt: A technician is recovering refrigerant from a small appliance chest freezer containing 5.8 ounces of R-404A using system-dependent recovery methods. The compressor operates normally and the recovery gauge shows 1 inch of mercury vacuum. What must happen before the recovery process can be considered complete?

options.a: Recovery is complete, since any vacuum reading meets the small-appliance level
options.b: Keep recovering until the gauge holds at 10 inches of mercury vacuum
options.c: Recover 90% of the charge or pull the unit down to 4 inches Hg vacuum
options.d: Stop once 80% of the charge is out, the level for a running compressor

epa-608-readiness-check-type-1-050.explanation: With recovery equipment made after November 15, 1993 and a running compressor, a small appliance must have 90% of its charge recovered or be evacuated to 4 inches of Hg vacuum. A 1-inch reading has not reached that level, so recovery continues.

distractorExplanations.a: A 1-inch vacuum is shallower than the 4-inch small-appliance level, and with no percentage check the job is not complete.
distractorExplanations.b: 10 inches Hg vacuum is a high-pressure appliance level from the evacuation table, not the small-appliance requirement.
distractorExplanations.d: 80% is the share for a compressor that does not run; with a working compressor the figure is 90% or a 4-inch vacuum.

options.a: Recover 70% of the charge, the minimum when the compressor will not run
options.b: Recover 80% of the charge or evacuate the unit to 4 inches Hg vacuum
options.c: Cut the refrigerant lines and let the 4-ounce charge dissipate outdoors
options.d: Notify EPA within 30 days, then recover the refrigerant at the scrap yard

epa-608-readiness-check-type-1-027.explanation: Before a small appliance is scrapped, its refrigerant must be recovered. With the compressor not running, recovery equipment made after November 15, 1993 must remove 80% of the charge or pull the unit to 4 inches of Hg vacuum; a 4-ounce charge is not exempt.

distractorExplanations.a: With a non-operating compressor the small-appliance requirement is 80% recovery, not 70%.
distractorExplanations.c: Small charges are not exempt from the venting prohibition; refrigerant must be recovered before disposal.
distractorExplanations.d: EPA does not require disposal notification; the refrigerant must be recovered (or recovery verified) before disposal.

options.a: System-dependent recovery equipment certified to recover 70% of refrigerant
options.b: Equipment certified to recover 90% of the charge or pull a 4-inch vacuum
options.c: Any recovery equipment capable of achieving 15 inches mercury vacuum
options.d: Self-contained recovery equipment certified to recover 95% of refrigerant

epa-608-readiness-check-type-1-047.explanation: An 11-ounce factory-sealed cooler is a small appliance. Recovery equipment made after November 15, 1993 must be certified to recover 90% of the charge when the compressor runs (80% when it does not) or to reach 4 inches of Hg vacuum; there is no special rule for charges over 10 ounces.

distractorExplanations.a: 70% is not an EPA small-appliance recovery level; the options are 80% or 90% depending on compressor status.
distractorExplanations.c: 15 inches Hg vacuum is the level for high-pressure appliances of 200 pounds or more, not the small-appliance standard.
distractorExplanations.d: 95% is not a Section 608 figure; small-appliance equipment is certified to 90% (compressor on), 80% (off) or 4 inches of vacuum.

epa-608-readiness-check-type-2-045.prompt: A technician must replace the evaporator coil in a packaged rooftop unit containing 28 pounds of R-410A. The recovery machine was manufactured in 2021, and the system is operating normally with standard pressures. What recovery action is required before opening the system?

options.a: No recovery, since a coil swap on a normally running unit counts as routine maintenance
options.b: Recover to 0 psig, since the unit holds less than 200 pounds of refrigerant
options.c: Recover refrigerant to 10 inches of mercury vacuum before opening the system
options.d: Recover refrigerant to 15 inches of mercury vacuum throughout the entire system

epa-608-readiness-check-type-2-045.explanation: R-410A falls in the 'other high-pressure' row of the evacuation table. For a unit holding less than 200 pounds, recovery equipment made after November 15, 1993 must pull 10 inches of Hg vacuum before a major repair such as an evaporator coil swap (4 inches with older equipment); 15 inches applies at 200 pounds or more.

distractorExplanations.a: Replacing an evaporator coil is a major repair under Section 608, so the circuit must be recovered to the required level first.
distractorExplanations.b: 0 psig is the level for R-22 appliances under 200 pounds; R-410A falls in the other high-pressure row, which needs 10 inches.
distractorExplanations.d: 15 inches Hg vacuum applies to other high-pressure appliances holding 200 pounds or more, not a 28-pound rooftop unit.

epa-608-readiness-check-type-3-044.prompt: Using recovery equipment manufactured after November 15, 1993, what evacuation level must a low-pressure appliance reach before it is opened for a major repair?

options.a: 15 inches of mercury vacuum
options.b: 25 inches of mercury vacuum
options.c: 25 millimeters of mercury absolute
options.d: 500 microns (0.5 mm) of mercury absolute

epa-608-readiness-check-type-3-044.explanation: Section 608's evacuation table sets low-pressure appliances at 25 mm Hg absolute when the recovery equipment was made on or after November 15, 1993 (25 inches Hg vacuum for older machines). 25 mm absolute is roughly 29 inches of vacuum, so it is the deeper of the two levels.

distractorExplanations.a: 15 inches Hg vacuum is the level for high- or medium-pressure appliances of 200 pounds or more, not for low-pressure chillers.
distractorExplanations.b: 25 inches Hg vacuum is the level for recovery equipment made before November 15, 1993; newer machines must reach 25 mm absolute.
distractorExplanations.d: 500 microns is a dehydration target used before charging, not the Section 608 recovery level for opening a low-pressure appliance.

epa-608-readiness-check-type-2-007.prompt: Why do cylinders of flammable A2L refrigerants such as R-32 and R-454B have left-hand (reverse) threaded valves?

options.a: To keep hoses and gear built for nonflammable gases from being connected
options.b: Because A2L blends must be charged as vapor, and the valve meters vapor flow
options.c: To increase recovery speed on high-pressure systems
options.d: Because left-hand threads hold the higher A2L cylinder pressure without leaking

epa-608-readiness-check-type-2-007.explanation: Cylinders of flammable refrigerants, including A2Ls like R-32 and R-454B, use left-hand threaded valves (and a red band) so hoses, recovery machines and gauges meant for nonflammable refrigerants such as R-410A cannot be connected by mistake. R-410A cylinders keep standard right-hand threads.

distractorExplanations.b: R-454B is a blend charged as liquid and R-32 is a single compound; thread direction has nothing to do with vapor metering.
distractorExplanations.c: Thread orientation is a safety and compatibility measure, not a recovery-speed feature.
distractorExplanations.d: Thread direction does not change pressure rating; cylinder pressure capacity comes from the DOT cylinder specification.

epa-608-readiness-check-core-035.prompt: A commercial refrigeration system holds 18 pounds of R-502. A leak has let 3 pounds escape over 6 months, about 33% per year. What do the Section 608 leak repair requirements say about this system?

options.a: Repair within 30 days, because 33% is above the 20% commercial trigger rate
options.b: Shut the system down at once, because R-502 is a phased-out CFC blend
options.c: Repair within 12 months, the deadline for commercial refrigeration leaks
options.d: No repair deadline applies; the charge is under the 50-pound threshold

epa-608-readiness-check-core-035.explanation: Section 608 leak repair duties apply to ODS appliances with a full charge of 50 pounds or more. At 18 pounds no repair deadline is triggered, even though 33% would exceed the 20% commercial refrigeration rate on a larger system; venting is still prohibited whenever the system is serviced.

distractorExplanations.a: The 20% commercial refrigeration trigger applies to appliances holding 50 pounds or more; this system has 18 pounds.
distractorExplanations.b: R-502 production has ended, but Section 608 has no immediate-shutdown requirement for leaks in a small commercial system.
distractorExplanations.c: There is no 12-month repair deadline; one year is the window to complete a retrofit or retirement plan on large appliances.

epa-608-readiness-check-core-050.prompt: A technician discovers that a commercial refrigeration system containing 60 pounds of R-22 has been leaking. Maintenance records show that 18 pounds of refrigerant were added during the past 12 months to maintain proper operation. What is the required action under EPA Section 608 regulations?
epa-608-readiness-check-core-050.explanation: 18 pounds added to a 60-pound full charge is a 30% annual leak rate, above the 20% trigger for commercial refrigeration appliances holding 50 pounds or more of an ODS refrigerant. The owner must repair the leak within 30 days or create a retrofit or retirement plan within 30 days and complete it within one year.

distractorExplanations.a: 30% is above the 20% commercial refrigeration trigger rate, so continuing to run without repair or a plan is not allowed.

epa-608-readiness-check-type-1-028.prompt: A technician is servicing a reach-in cooler, a factory-sealed unit holding 12 ounces of R-22. Electronic leak detection finds a significant leak at a brazed joint in the evaporator. The compressor runs normally, and the owner wants the joint re-brazed. What does EPA Section 608 require of the technician?

options.a: Recover the charge to the small-appliance level before opening the joint
options.b: Repair the leak within 30 days, the deadline set for small appliances
options.c: Replace the entire evaporator coil since brazing repairs are prohibited
options.d: Log the leak and report it to EPA before scheduling the repair

epa-608-readiness-check-type-1-028.explanation: Section 608 sets no leak repair deadline for small appliances, but refrigerant may not be vented. Before the joint is opened for brazing, the charge must be recovered to the small-appliance level: 90% with the compressor running (equipment made after November 15, 1993) or 4 inches of Hg vacuum.

distractorExplanations.b: Leak repair deadlines apply to appliances of 50 pounds or more; Section 608 sets no 30-day repair clock for small appliances.
distractorExplanations.c: Brazing repairs are acceptable and commonly used for refrigeration leak repairs when performed by qualified technicians.
distractorExplanations.d: EPA has no leak-reporting requirement for small appliances; the duty is to recover the charge before opening the joint.

epa-608-readiness-check-type-1-034.prompt: A technician services a small appliance ice machine holding 11 ounces of R-404A. The condenser coil needs cleaning, the compressor runs normally, and a small leak is found at a flare fitting. Which statement describes the EPA Section 608 rules for this leak?

options.a: A 30-day repair deadline applies, since any detected leak triggers repair
options.b: The leak must be reported to EPA within 30 days, then fixed at the next visit
options.c: Repair is due within 12 months, the deadline for appliances under 50 pounds
options.d: No repair deadline applies, but venting is barred if the fitting is opened

epa-608-readiness-check-type-1-034.explanation: Section 608 leak repair requirements apply to appliances with 50 pounds or more of an ODS refrigerant, so this 11-ounce small appliance has no federal repair deadline. The venting prohibition still applies: if the flare fitting is opened, the refrigerant must be recovered first. Fixing the leak is still good practice.

distractorExplanations.a: Leak repair deadlines are tied to appliances holding 50 pounds or more; a small leak in an 11-ounce unit triggers no 30-day clock.
distractorExplanations.b: EPA has no leak report for small appliances; reporting duties attach to large appliances that miss repair deadlines or leak chronically.
distractorExplanations.c: There is no 12-month repair rule for small appliances; Section 608 sets no repair deadline below 50 pounds.

epa-608-readiness-check-type-1-004.prompt: How does the evacuation level for small appliances compare with the levels set for larger high-pressure appliances under Section 608?

options.a: It is deeper: small appliances must reach 25 mm Hg absolute, like chillers
options.b: It is the same: every appliance type is pulled to 10 inches of Hg vacuum
options.c: No level is set; recovery from a small appliance stops when gauges read 0 psig
options.d: It is shallower: 4 inches Hg vacuum versus up to 15 inches for larger units

epa-608-readiness-check-type-1-004.explanation: Small appliances meet Section 608 by recovering 80-90% of the charge or by reaching 4 inches of Hg vacuum. Larger high-pressure appliances need 0 psig (R-22 under 200 lb), 10 inches or 15 inches depending on refrigerant, charge size and equipment date, so the small-appliance vacuum is shallower.

distractorExplanations.a: 25 mm Hg absolute is the low-pressure chiller level for newer recovery equipment, not the small-appliance requirement.
distractorExplanations.b: Levels differ by appliance type; 10 inches applies to some high-pressure units, while small appliances use 4 inches or a percentage.
distractorExplanations.c: Small appliances do have a level: 80% or 90% of the charge recovered, or 4 inches of Hg vacuum, not 0 psig.

epa-608-readiness-check-type-1-031.prompt: A technician recovers the refrigerant from a 7-ounce R-22 dehumidifier with a burned-out compressor before the unit goes to a scrap recycler. What lets the recycler accept the unit without recovering the refrigerant itself?

options.a: Draining the compressor oil and shipping it with the refrigerant for reclaim
options.b: Flushing the system with nitrogen and tagging it as free of refrigerant
options.c: Installing locking caps on the service ports to deter refrigerant theft
options.d: A signed statement with the recoverer's name, address and recovery date

epa-608-readiness-check-type-1-031.explanation: Under the safe disposal rule, the final processor (scrap recycler) must recover the refrigerant or verify it was already recovered, usually with a signed statement giving the name and address of the person who recovered it and the date, or a contract stating removal happens before delivery.

distractorExplanations.a: Reclaimers process refrigerant, not compressor oil; draining oil does not show the recycler that the charge was recovered.
distractorExplanations.b: A nitrogen flush and a tag are not the verification the safe disposal rule calls for, and flushing is not a disposal requirement.
distractorExplanations.c: Locking caps are a building-code anti-tamper measure for outdoor units, not disposal verification for a small appliance.

epa-608-readiness-check-type-3-007.prompt: Which type of recovery equipment is appropriate for removing the charge from a low-pressure centrifugal chiller holding 900 pounds of R-123?

options.a: Self-contained machines built for low-pressure refrigerants
options.b: System-dependent recovery that relies on the chiller's own compressor
options.c: Passive recovery bags without active pumping or a condenser
options.d: Standard high-pressure recovery machines rated for 400 psig cylinders

epa-608-readiness-check-type-3-007.explanation: System-dependent (passive) recovery may be used only on appliances holding 15 pounds or less, so a 900-pound chiller needs self-contained equipment. Machines for R-123 chillers recover liquid first and then pull vapor down to the low-pressure evacuation level (25 mm Hg absolute).

distractorExplanations.b: System-dependent recovery is limited to appliances with 15 pounds or less of refrigerant, so it cannot be used on a 900-pound chiller.
distractorExplanations.c: Passive bags are a small-appliance technique and cannot reach the deep vacuum levels set for low-pressure chillers.
distractorExplanations.d: High-pressure machines are not designed for the sub-atmospheric conditions and large liquid volumes of low-pressure chillers.

epa-608-readiness-check-type-3-026.prompt: When recovering refrigerant from a low-pressure appliance, why must hose connections and recovery equipment be kept leak-tight?
epa-608-readiness-check-type-3-026.explanation: Much of a low-pressure appliance runs below atmospheric pressure, and recovery pulls it deeper into vacuum, so any loose fitting draws air inward rather than leaking refrigerant out. That air is a non-condensable that contaminates the recovered refrigerant and raises condensing pressure.

options.a: Recover the liquid first, then recover the remaining vapor
options.b: Run the purge unit to vent the refrigerant vapor before opening the shell
options.c: Pressurize the shell with nitrogen to 50 psig to push out the liquid
options.d: Drain the oil from the sump first, then recover the vapor from the condenser

epa-608-readiness-check-type-3-016.explanation: On a low-pressure chiller, recovery starts by removing liquid refrigerant, because most of the charge sits as liquid, and then vapor is recovered down to the required level (25 mm Hg absolute with newer equipment). Heating the vessel can speed up the vapor stage.

distractorExplanations.b: The purge unit removes non-condensables, not the charge; using it to vent refrigerant is prohibited.
distractorExplanations.c: 50 psig exceeds the roughly 15 psig rupture disc on a low-pressure chiller and mixes nitrogen into the refrigerant.
distractorExplanations.d: Oil holds dissolved refrigerant and is removed after recovery; recovery starts with the refrigerant charge.

options.a: The mixed refrigerant can be reused in any compatible system after proper filtration
options.b: The mixture must be reclaimed to AHRI 700 standards or sent for destruction
options.c: Only the R-22 portion needs to be reclaimed; the R-134a can be vented safely
options.d: The mixture can be separated using standard recovery equipment and reused immediately

epa-608-readiness-check-core-025.explanation: Mixed refrigerants cannot be reused as-is. Recovered refrigerant sold to a new owner must be reclaimed to AHRI Standard 700 purity by an EPA-certified reclaimer; a mixed R-22/R-134a batch that cannot be separated is sent for destruction.

distractorExplanations.a: Mixed refrigerants have altered thermodynamic properties and cannot be safely reused even with filtration, as this doesn't address the fundamental contamination issue.
distractorExplanations.c: All regulated refrigerants, including R-134a, are subject to EPA venting prohibitions and cannot be released to the atmosphere regardless of contamination status.
distractorExplanations.d: Standard recovery equipment cannot effectively separate different refrigerant types, and even if separation were possible, the refrigerants would still require proper reclamation before reuse.

epa-608-readiness-check-core-026.prompt: Which refrigerants are covered by the Section 608 venting prohibition and recovery requirements?
epa-608-readiness-check-core-026.explanation: Section 608 began with ozone-depleting CFCs and HCFCs, and its venting prohibition and recovery rules also cover their substitutes, including HFCs, even though HFCs have zero ODP and are regulated for their global warming impact.

options.a: Use the equipment as-is, since the small R-22 residue is within AHRI 700 purity limits
options.b: Flush the recovery equipment with nitrogen and vent it before switching refrigerant types
options.c: Evacuate the machine into the R-22 cylinder, then use a separate cylinder for R-134a
options.d: Change the filter-drier and hoses, then connect directly to the R-134a system without evacuating

epa-608-readiness-check-core-027.explanation: Before switching refrigerants, the recovery machine is pumped out (self-evacuated) so residual R-22 goes into the R-22 recovery cylinder, the filter is changed per the manufacturer, and a separate recovery cylinder is used for the R-134a so the two never mix.

distractorExplanations.a: AHRI 700 is a reclaim purity standard, not a tolerance for residue; leftover R-22 contaminates the R-134a.
distractorExplanations.b: A nitrogen flush does not pull residual refrigerant and oil out of the machine and venting it releases refrigerant.
distractorExplanations.d: New hoses and a filter-drier do not remove R-22 left in the machine's compressor and condenser; evacuation is still needed.

options.a: The system has leaked its charge, so it can be opened after a 0 psig gauge check
options.b: The gauges are reading falsely low, so the system should be pressurized with nitrogen first
options.c: Vapor and oil-dissolved refrigerant may remain, so recovery should still be done
options.d: The charge has migrated to the compressor crankcase, so only the oil needs recovery

epa-608-readiness-check-type-2-026.explanation: A 0 psig reading means the system is at atmospheric pressure, not empty: refrigerant vapor stays in the lines and coils and some is dissolved in the oil. The system must still be recovered to the required evacuation level (or as far as leaks allow) before it is opened.

distractorExplanations.a: A 0 psig reading does not prove the system is empty; refrigerant can remain and recovery must still be attempted.
distractorExplanations.b: Adding nitrogen to a system that may still hold refrigerant creates a mixture that is later vented.
distractorExplanations.d: Refrigerant vapor in the lines and coils must be recovered along with the refrigerant dissolved in the oil.

epa-608-readiness-check-core-002.prompt: Using recovery equipment made after November 15, 1993, what share of the charge must be recovered from a small appliance whose compressor is operating, if the 4-inch vacuum option is not used?
epa-608-readiness-check-core-002.explanation: For small appliances, recovery equipment made after November 15, 1993 must recover 90% of the charge when the compressor is operating and 80% when it is not, or evacuate the appliance to 4 inches of Hg vacuum. Larger stationary equipment uses the vacuum table, not a percentage.

distractorExplanations.a: 80% is the small-appliance figure when the compressor is not operating (or for pre-1993 equipment), not when it runs.
distractorExplanations.b: 85% is not a figure in the Section 608 small-appliance rule; the choices are 90% or 80% depending on compressor status.
distractorExplanations.d: 95% is not required in the small-appliance rule; 90% with a running compressor, or a 4-inch vacuum, satisfies it.

options.a: High pressure rating above 200 psi
options.b: Ozone depletion potential (ODP) greater than zero
options.c: Flammability safety classification of A2 or A3
options.d: Toxicity level exceeding OSHA exposure standards

epa-608-readiness-check-core-010.explanation: Section 608 was written around ozone-depleting substances, so ODP above zero is the classic trigger and the reason CFCs and HCFCs are covered. Since the 2016 rule, its venting prohibition and recovery requirements also extend to substitutes such as HFCs, which have zero ODP.

distractorExplanations.a: Pressure rating alone does not determine EPA 608 applicability; many high-pressure refrigerants are not ozone-depleting.
distractorExplanations.c: Flammability classification affects safety codes and equipment standards but not EPA 608 coverage, which grew out of ozone protection.
distractorExplanations.d: OSHA toxicity and exposure standards are workplace rules, separate from the EPA environmental regulations under Section 608.

distractorExplanations.a: 8 pounds is over the 5-pound small-appliance limit, and a commercial ice machine of that size is not a factory-sealed small appliance.

epa-608-readiness-check-core-009.prompt: A technician will open an R-22 comfort cooling appliance holding 300 pounds of refrigerant for a major repair, using recovery equipment made in 2018. What must be done before refrigerant-containing connections are broken?
epa-608-readiness-check-core-009.explanation: R-22 appliances holding 200 pounds or more must be evacuated to 10 inches of Hg vacuum with recovery equipment made on or after November 15, 1993 (4 inches with older equipment). 0 psig is the level for R-22 units under 200 pounds, and 15 inches applies to other high-pressure refrigerants at 200 pounds or more.

distractorExplanations.a: 0 psig is the level for R-22 appliances under 200 pounds; at 300 pounds the R-22 level is 10 inches Hg vacuum.
distractorExplanations.c: 15 inches applies to other high-pressure refrigerants such as R-410A at 200 pounds or more, not to R-22.
distractorExplanations.d: Intentional venting of refrigerant is prohibited under the Clean Air Act and can result in significant EPA penalties.

epa-608-readiness-check-core-016.prompt: Before an R-410A appliance holding 250 pounds is sent for disposal, what level must recovery equipment made after November 15, 1993 reach?

options.a: 0 psig (atmospheric pressure)
options.b: 4 inches of mercury vacuum
options.c: 10 inches of mercury vacuum

distractorExplanations.b: 15% was the comfort cooling trigger before the 2016 rule took effect; it does not apply to industrial process chillers.

epa-608-readiness-check-type-3-021.prompt: A low-pressure chiller used for building comfort cooling holds 75 pounds of R-123. What annual leak rate triggers the 30-day repair requirement?
epa-608-readiness-check-type-3-021.explanation: Low-pressure chillers follow the trigger for their use. A comfort cooling appliance holding 50 pounds or more of an ODS refrigerant such as R-123 must be repaired once its annual leak rate exceeds 10%.

distractorExplanations.b: 15% was the comfort cooling trigger before the 2016 rule took effect; the current rate is 10%.
distractorExplanations.c: 20% is the commercial refrigeration trigger, not the rate for a comfort cooling chiller.
distractorExplanations.d: 35% was the old commercial and industrial trigger; industrial process refrigeration now uses 30%.

epa-608-readiness-check-type-3-040.prompt: What sets the leak repair trigger rate for a low-pressure chiller holding 50 pounds or more of R-123?

options.a: Its use category, such as comfort cooling or industrial process
options.b: Its pressure class, with low-pressure units allowed a 35% rate
options.c: Its refrigerant's ODP, with R-123 allowed a 20% rate
options.d: Its age, with chillers built before 1993 allowed a 15% rate

epa-608-readiness-check-type-3-040.explanation: Section 608 trigger rates follow how the appliance is used: 10% for comfort cooling, 20% for commercial refrigeration and 30% for industrial process refrigeration. A low-pressure chiller gets no special rate because of its pressure class or refrigerant.

distractorExplanations.b: There is no low-pressure category; 35% was the old commercial and industrial trigger and no longer applies.
distractorExplanations.c: Trigger rates do not depend on ODP; 20% is the commercial refrigeration rate.
distractorExplanations.d: Equipment age does not set the trigger; 15% was the comfort cooling rate before the 2016 rule.

epa-608-readiness-check-type-3-023.prompt: A low-pressure chiller used for comfort cooling holds 600 pounds of R-123 and exceeded its leak trigger rate. After the repair, how often must it be inspected for leaks under the 2016 rule?
epa-608-readiness-check-type-3-023.explanation: Under the 2016 rule, a comfort cooling appliance holding 50 pounds or more that exceeded its trigger rate must be leak inspected once a year until it stays below the trigger for a year. Quarterly inspections apply to commercial and industrial systems of 500 pounds or more.

distractorExplanations.a: Monthly inspections are not a Section 608 requirement for comfort cooling chillers.
distractorExplanations.b: Quarterly inspections apply to commercial refrigeration and industrial process systems of 500 pounds or more, not comfort cooling.

epa-608-readiness-check-type-3-029.prompt: After a low-pressure chiller opened for major repairs is evacuated, why is refrigerant charged as vapor first before liquid?

options.a: Vapor sweeps out the air the vacuum pump left behind
options.b: Liquid charging is limited by EPA to 25 pounds per hour
options.c: Liquid flashing in a deep vacuum can freeze water in the tubes
options.d: Vapor charging keeps oil from foaming out of the compressor

epa-608-readiness-check-type-3-029.explanation: In a deep vacuum, liquid refrigerant flashes and its temperature drops below freezing, which can freeze and burst water tubes. Charging vapor first raises the pressure above the saturation point for 32°F before liquid is added.

distractorExplanations.a: Sweeping air out with refrigerant vents refrigerant; air must be removed by evacuation before charging.
distractorExplanations.b: EPA sets no charging rate limit; the vapor-first step protects the tubes from freezing.
distractorExplanations.d: Oil foaming is not the reason; vapor first raises pressure so flashing liquid will not freeze the tube water.

epa-608-readiness-check-type-3-030.prompt: Which condition is most likely to make a low-pressure chiller's evaporator run at a deeper vacuum than normal during the cooling season?

options.a: Heavily fouled condenser tubes
options.b: Low refrigerant charge
options.c: Compressor motor burnout
options.d: Expansion valve stuck open

epa-608-readiness-check-type-3-030.explanation: With less refrigerant in the evaporator, its saturation pressure and temperature fall, so it runs at a deeper vacuum than normal. A failed purge unit acts on the high side instead: trapped non-condensables raise condenser pressure.

distractorExplanations.a: Fouled condenser tubes raise head pressure; they do not pull the evaporator into a deeper vacuum.
distractorExplanations.c: A compressor motor burnout would prevent system operation entirely rather than cause deeper vacuum operation.
distractorExplanations.d: An expansion valve stuck open floods the evaporator and raises its pressure rather than deepening the vacuum.

epa-608-readiness-check-type-3-036.prompt: During refrigerant recovery from a low-pressure appliance, what vacuum level must recovery equipment manufactured before November 15, 1993 achieve?
epa-608-readiness-check-type-3-036.explanation: For low-pressure appliances, recovery equipment made before November 15, 1993 must reach 25 inches of Hg vacuum. Equipment made on or after that date must reach the deeper 25 mm Hg absolute, which is about 29 inches of vacuum.

distractorExplanations.a: 10 inches is a high-pressure appliance level, far too shallow for a low-pressure chiller.
distractorExplanations.b: 15 inches is the level for high-pressure appliances of 200 pounds or more, not low-pressure chillers.
distractorExplanations.d: About 29 inches (25 mm Hg absolute) is the level for newer equipment; pre-1993 machines must reach 25 inches.

epa-608-readiness-check-type-3-045.prompt: Which job on a low-pressure chiller counts as a major repair under Section 608, requiring evacuation to the full low-pressure level first?

options.a: Replacing a gasket on the purge unit's pump-out line
options.b: Removing the condenser for retubing
options.c: Replacing the float valve's access cover gasket
options.d: Changing the oil filter on the oil pump circuit

epa-608-readiness-check-type-3-045.explanation: Section 608 defines a major repair as one that removes the compressor, condenser, evaporator or an auxiliary heat exchanger coil. Removing the condenser for retubing qualifies, so the chiller must first be evacuated to 25 mm Hg absolute (with equipment made after November 15, 1993).

distractorExplanations.a: A purge-line gasket does not remove a major component, so replacing it is a non-major repair.
distractorExplanations.c: Replacing a cover gasket does not remove the compressor, condenser, evaporator or a heat exchanger coil.
distractorExplanations.d: An oil filter change is a non-major repair; major repairs remove a major component such as the condenser.

epa-608-readiness-check-type-3-047.prompt: How does Section 608 define the refrigerant used in a low-pressure appliance?

options.a: Evaporator pressure below 10 psig at full load
options.b: Saturation pressure below 45 psia at 104°F
options.c: Saturation pressure of 45 to 170 psia at 104°F
options.d: Saturation pressure of 170 to 355 psia at 104°F

epa-608-readiness-check-type-3-047.explanation: A low-pressure appliance uses a refrigerant whose liquid-phase saturation pressure is below 45 psia at 104°F, such as R-123 or R-11. Medium-pressure refrigerants fall between 45 and 170 psia, and high-pressure ones between 170 and 355 psia.

distractorExplanations.a: Section 608 defines pressure classes by saturation pressure at 104°F, not by evaporator gauge pressure.
distractorExplanations.c: 45 to 170 psia at 104°F is the medium-pressure range, which includes refrigerants such as R-134a.
distractorExplanations.d: 170 to 355 psia at 104°F is the high-pressure range, which includes refrigerants such as R-22 and R-404A.

epa-608-readiness-check-type-3-049.prompt: What evacuation requirement applies when recovering refrigerant from a low-pressure chiller with recovery equipment made after November 15, 1993?

options.a: Recovery is not required if the appliance contains less than 15 pounds of refrigerant
options.b: The appliance must be isolated and the refrigerant allowed to self-evacuate to atmospheric pressure
options.c: Recovery must continue until the appliance pressure reaches 0 psig or below
options.d: Recovery equipment must pull the appliance down to 25 millimeters of mercury absolute

epa-608-readiness-check-type-3-049.explanation: With recovery equipment made after November 15, 1993, low-pressure appliances must be evacuated to 25 mm Hg absolute (about 29 inches of vacuum); older equipment must reach 25 inches Hg vacuum. Low-pressure chillers hold far more than 15 pounds, so self-contained equipment is used.

distractorExplanations.a: Recovery is required regardless of refrigerant quantity in low-pressure appliances during service or disposal.
distractorExplanations.b: Passive self-evacuation to atmospheric pressure is insufficient and violates EPA recovery requirements for low-pressure systems.
distractorExplanations.c: Reaching 0 psig is insufficient for low-pressure appliances, which require evacuation to vacuum levels well below atmospheric pressure.
